\setcounter{chapter}{5}

\chapter*{\raggedright\Huge MEASUREMENT\\OF SEGMENTS}
\addcontentsline{toc}{chapter}{5.\ Measurement of Segments}
\markboth{MEASUREMENT OF SEGMENTS}{}
\vspace{-1em}\noindent\rule{\linewidth}{0.6pt}\vspace{1em}
\figurekey

%========================================================= 5-1
\section*{5--1\quad INTRODUCTION}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{5--1\quad Introduction}

In this chapter we are going to get a number for the length of a segment, that
is for the distance between two points. The way we get the length will be
exactly the same as the method we use in practical work. We will see that
finding a length is based upon simple \emph{counting}. For example, when you
pace off the length of a building (Fig.~5--1), you count how many steps you
take. Or when you say that the room is 15 feet wide, you mean that a foot ruler
can be laid down 15 times, one after the other, on a line. If the width of the
room is between 14 and 15 feet, the ruler can be laid down 14 times, but 15
times would put the end of the ruler past the wall. To measure the room more
accurately, you must choose a smaller unit of measure, say an inch, so that if
the width is 14 feet and three inches, the foot ruler can be laid down 14 times
and beyond that the inch ruler can be laid down three times. If even then you
have not come exactly to the wall of the room, you must choose an even smaller
unit of measure, some fraction of an inch, and so on.

\FIGVONE

\exercisegroup{5--1}

\begin{multicols}{2}
\begin{exlist}
\item Measure the length of your desk. Describe the process of measurement in
      terms of counting.
\item Measure the length of a page. Describe the counting you do to get the
      length.
\item Think of other examples of measurement and describe them in terms of
      counting.
\end{exlist}
\end{multicols}

%========================================================= 5-2
\section*{5--2\quad NUMBERS}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{5--2\quad Numbers}

Because we express length in terms of numbers, we need certain facts about
numbers that you learned in algebra and arithmetic. You have studied different
kinds of numbers. In the beginning grades you first used whole numbers
$1$, $2,\ldots$ and learned how to add, subtract, and multiply them. These
numbers we now call the \emph{positive integers} instead of ``whole numbers.''
When you tried to divide integers you found that it was necessary to have other
numbers, which you called \emph{fractions}, for example,
$\frac{1}{2}$, $\frac{2}{3}$, $\frac{5}{8}$, $\frac{7}{37}$. These are numbers
obtained by dividing one integer by another integer. \emph{The numbers which
are either positive integers or positive fractions are called positive rational
numbers.}

You also wrote numbers as \emph{decimals}, for example, 1.25, 2.537, 173.612.
Sometimes a rational number when written as a decimal ``comes out even,'' as
for example, $\frac{1}{2} = 0.5$, $\frac{3}{8} = 0.375$. Sometimes it does not
come out even, so that the decimal goes on forever, for example,
$\frac{1}{3} = 0.333\ldots$, $\frac{2}{3} = 0.6666\ldots$,
$\frac{1}{11} = 0.090909\ldots$. You also met with other numbers which did not
come out even, for example, $\sqrt{2} = 1.4142\ldots$,
$\sqrt{3} = 1.7321\ldots$. These numbers are different from $\frac{1}{3}$,
$\frac{2}{3}$, and $\frac{1}{11}$ because they not only do not come out even,
but \emph{the decimal never repeats}. In other words, no matter to how many
decimal places you were to calculate $\sqrt{2}$, you would never reach a place
where, from then on, one group of digits would occur over and over again in the
same order.

Decimals that, after some place, repeat one group of digits over and over are
called \emph{repeating decimals}. Decimals which come out even are called
\emph{terminating decimals}, and may be considered as repeating with zeros.

\exercise{5--2}

Write the following rational numbers as decimals to see that they are repeating
decimals. If they come out even (terminate), the repeating part is all zeros.
1/6, 5/6, 122/99, 1/13, 1/7, 6/5, 3/2.

\medskip
It is proved in advanced algebra that rational numbers are always repeating
decimals, and that, conversely, repeating decimals are rational numbers. (These
proofs are hard, so don't be discouraged if you cannot construct them; your
teacher may show you.) Hence, rational numbers and repeating decimals are the
same. What, then, about the decimals which never repeat? These numbers are not
rational numbers, and so they have been called \emph{irrational
numbers}.*%
\Vstarfoot{The word ``irrational'' is not a very pleasant choice
because it sounds like ``not sensible.'' What it really means is this. Rational
numbers are obtained by dividing one integer by another; that is, a rational
number is the ratio of two integers. Hence the word ``rational'' in ``rational
number'' means that the number is a \emph{ratio} of integers. Therefore, an
\emph{irrational} number is one which is \emph{not} the ratio of two integers.}
Irrational numbers are defined to be \emph{those numbers which are not
rational}. Examples of irrational numbers are $\sqrt{2}$, $\sqrt{3}$,
$\sqrt{5}$, $\sqrt[3]{2}$, $\sqrt[3]{17}$, and, in fact, any root of an integer
which is not itself an integer.

All the decimals together are defined to be the \emph{real numbers}. Thus a
real number is a decimal. If the decimal repeats, the number is a rational
number. If the decimal does not repeat, it is an irrational number.

\exercisegroup{5--3}
% Book p.75 holds this chapter's first starred exercises (nos. 4 and 7) but
% prints NO "*Starred ... are optional" footnote -- verified against PDF p.89.
% ch02 owns the book-wide first use; deliberately no \starnote here.

\begin{multicols}{2}
\begin{exlist}
\item Write the symbols for several rational numbers and for several irrational
      numbers.
\item Is $3.131313\ldots$, where the 1's and 3's keep alternating, a rational
      number?
\item Is $0.234234234\ldots$, where 2, 3, and 4 keep following each other, a
      rational number?
\item[\stex 4.] The number $1.010010001\ldots$ is formed from just 0's and 1's.
      After each 1 there is one more 0 than the previous time. Is this number
      rational?
\item[5.] Give the definitions of rational number, irrational number, real
      number.
\item[6.] A real number is either rational or irrational. Why?
\item[\stex 7.] There is a rule for deciding when a fraction written as a
      decimal will have its repeating part all zeros and when it will not. For
      example, each of the fractions 3/20, 17/250, 5/16, and 4/25 has its
      repeating decimal part all zeros. The fractions 7/15, 5/12, and 11/23 do
      not. Can you discover the rule?
\end{exlist}
\end{multicols}

When we write a decimal, for example 1.23, we mean $1 + 0.2 + 0.03$ or
$1 + 2/10 + 3/100$. Similarly, $4.383 = 4 + 3/10 + 8/100 + 3/1000$. Thus, any
terminating decimal (one which comes out even) may be written as a sum of
ordinary fractions with denominators 10, $100,\ldots$. If the decimal is
repeating, this sum is an \emph{infinite} one, for example,
$1/3 = 0.333\ldots = 3/10 + 3/100 + 3/1000 + 3/10000 + \cdots$.

\exercisegroup{5--4}

\begin{multicols}{2}
\begin{exlist}
\item Write the following decimals as sums of rational numbers: 4.82, 1.29,
      2.75, 7.122, 0.8875, 2.40. In order to express each number as a single
      fraction, add the rational numbers.
\item Write the following numbers as decimals: $3 + 2/10 + 4/100$,
      $2 + 3/10 + 5/100 + 6/1000$, $4 + 3/100$, $1 + 1/10 + 1/10000$.
\item Write the following repeating decimals as sums of rational numbers:
      $0.6666\ldots$, $0.7777\ldots$, $0.121212\ldots$.
\item Write the following numbers as decimals:
      $1 + 2/10 + 2/100 + 2/1000 + \cdots$,
      $3 + 1/10 + 4/100 + 1/1000 + 4/10000 + \cdots$,
      $8/10 + 8/100 + 8/1000 + 8/10000 + \cdots$.
\end{exlist}
\end{multicols}

%========================================================= 5-3
\section*{5--3\quad INEQUALITIES}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{5--3\quad Inequalities}

In this book you are expected to know how to do arithmetic, that is, how to
add, subtract, multiply, and divide real numbers. But there is one part of
arithmetic you have not yet studied systematically. That part is concerned with
comparing the sizes of real numbers. Since you already know what it means to
say that the number $x$ is larger than the number $y$, all we need is a symbol
to indicate this. We therefore make the definition: $x > y$ means ``$x$ is
greater than $y$.'' Another way to say this is ``$x - y$ is a positive
number.'' We also define $x < y$ to mean ``$x$ is less than $y$,'' or, in other
words ``$y$ is greater than $x$.'' Listed below are several properties of real
numbers. These properties can be established as indicated in the review of
Chapter 4.

\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*), leftmargin=2.2em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=3pt]
\item If $x > y$ and $y = z$, then $x > z$.
\item If $x > y$ and $y > z$, then $x > z$.
\item $x$ is a positive number if and only if $x > 0$.
\item $x$ is a negative number if and only if $x < 0$.
\item If $x > y$, then $x - y > 0$, and conversely.
\end{enumerate}

\medskip
We define $x \geqq y$ to mean ``either $x > y$ or $x = y$,'' and we read
``$\geqq$'' as ``is greater than or equal to.'' We make a similar definition
for $x \leqq y$ (``$x$ is less than or equal to $y$'').

\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*), leftmargin=2.2em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=3pt,
                  start=6]
\item If $x > y$ and $u \geqq v$, then $x + u > y + v$.
\end{enumerate}

\exercisegroup{5--5}

\begin{multicols}{2}
\begin{exlist}
\item Substitute numbers for the variables in properties (a), (b), (e), and (f)
      above, and thus verify their truth for certain cases.
\item Write in symbols: $a$ is greater than $b$; $a$ is greater than or equal
      to $b$; $u$ is less than $w$; $a + c$ is less than or equal to $r + s$;
      $(a + b)^2$ is positive; $z$ is a negative number.
\item If $x$ is any real number, $x^2 \geqq 0$. Why?
\item Why is it true that if $x > 0$ and $y > 0$, then $xy > 0$?
\item Tell why $xy < 0$ if $x > 0$ and $y < 0$.
\end{exlist}
\end{multicols}

%========================================================= 5-4
\section*{5--4\quad MEASUREMENT}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{5--4\quad Measurement}

To measure a line segment we must first tell what our unit of length is. Some
units of length often used in practical work are inch, foot, yard, mile, meter,
centimeter, etc. Having picked a unit of length, we will describe the geometric
process whereby we get a real number, that is, a decimal for the length of a
line segment.

Choose any segment $CD$ as a unit (Fig.~5--2). This segment and all segments
congruent to it are defined to have length 1. Suppose $AB$ is any segment on a
line $l$. On the same side of $A$ as $B$ there is a point $A_1$ such that
$AA_1 \cong CD$. If $A_1 = B$, then the length of $AB$ is 1.

\FIGVTWO

\FIGVTHREE

\noindent If $B$ lies between $A$ and $A_1$ (Fig.~5--3), then our unit was too
large to measure the length of $AB$ in integers (whole numbers). We will return
to this possibility later. If $A_1$ lies between $A$ and $B$, then there is a
point $A_2$, on the same side of $A_1$ as $B$, such that either $A_2 = B$, or
$B$ is between $A_1$ and $A_2$, or $A_2$ is between $A_1$ and $B$. If
$A_2 = B$, the length of $AB$ is 2. If $B$ is between $A_1$ and $A_2$, then our
unit will not measure the length in integers. If $A_2$ is between $A_1$ and
$B$, there is a point $A_3$, on the same side of $A_2$ as $B$, such that
$A_2A_3 \cong CD$.

The process described above is what we actually follow when we measure. If we
lay out segments congruent to $CD$ from $A$ toward $B$, we know from experience
that we eventually either reach $B$ exactly, so that the length of $AB$ is an
integer, or reach a point \emph{beyond} $B$. Thus in Fig.~5--2, $A_4$ is beyond
$B$ but $A_3$ is still between $A$ and $B$. The length in this case will be a
number between 3 and 4. If the above process can always be carried out in our
geometry, then we have described the beginning of the process of measurement.

The only part of the above process that does not follow from our postulates is
the proof that we can always get to or beyond $B$. Because we need to do this,
we now add a new postulate to our list. It was the Greek mathematician
Archimedes (287--212 B.C.) who first stated this postulate. He apparently did
not see how to get it from Euclid's postulates and, needing it, assumed it was
true. It is one of the things that Euclid forgot to state as a postulate. It is
called \emph{Archimedes' axiom} or \emph{Archimedes' postulate} in spite of its
use by Eudoxus much earlier. This is the first of the two new postulates in
Postulate Group IV which we need for measurement. The other one will be given
later.

\medskip
IV--1 \emph{Archimedes' postulate.} If $AB$ is any segment on a line $l$ and
$CD$ any other segment, then there is a definite number $n$ of points
$A_1$, $A_2,\ldots$, $A_n$ on $l$ such that the points $A = A_0$, $A_1$,
$A_2,\ldots$, $A_n$ are arranged in this order, and all the segments $AA_1$,
$A_1A_2,\ldots$, $A_{n-1}A_n$ are congruent to $CD$, and either $B = A_n$ or
$B$ lies between $A_{n-1}$ and $A_n$.

\medskip
The integer $n$ is called \emph{Archimedes' integer}. When $n$ is 4, an
illustration would look like Fig.~5--4 or Fig.~5--5.

\FIGVFOURFIVE

\exercisegroup{5--6}

\begin{multicols}{2}
\begin{exlist}
\item If $AB$ is this segment \raisebox{0.18ex}{$A$\rule[0.35ex]{2.2em}{0.4pt}$B$}
      and $CD$ is this segment
      \raisebox{0.18ex}{$C$\rule[0.35ex]{1.3em}{0.4pt}$D$}, find how many
      points are needed to get beyond $B$.
\item Draw a segment $AB$ and a segment $CD$. Find the integer $n$ of
      Archimedes' axiom for your segments.
\end{exlist}
\end{multicols}

Using Archimedes' postulate, we find that the length of $AB$ is either an
integer or is between two integers. If the length lies between two integers,
the next step in the process is to divide the unit interval into tenths
(Fig.~5--6). (We would not have to keep to tenths if we were not trying to come
out with a decimal.) Then we count ``tenths'' until either we reach $B$ exactly
or $B$ lies between two of the tenth marks. If we reach $B$ exactly, then the
length of $AB$ comes out exactly in tenths. If $B$ is not reached exactly, then
we must divide the unit interval into one-hundredths and repeat the process. In
this way we obtain a real number or decimal, for the length of $AB$. In
Fig.~5--7 the length of $AB$ is about 2.3.

\FIGVSIXSEVEN

We have indicated a segment by writing the two endpoints of the segment as
$AB$. At this point we also need a notation for the \emph{length} of the
segment. For this we will use $\sg{AB}$, that is $\sg{AB} = $ \emph{the length
of the segment} $AB$. Whenever you see the symbol $\sg{AB}$ you must remember
that it represents a \emph{number}, while the symbol $AB$ stands for a \emph{set
of points}.

Except for dividing a segment into tenths, the entire procedure of this section
can be carried out (that is, described) in our geometry. At the moment we do
not have the means for dividing a segment into tenths. As soon as we have
studied parallel lines (Chapter 8), we will be able to make this construction.
Since we do not need the results of this chapter until after we have studied
parallel lines, our procedure is logically correct.

\exercisegroup{5--7}

\begin{multicols}{2}
\begin{exlist}
\item Draw a line segment. Then draw a segment that will be your unit. Now
      measure the first segment, describing how you use Archimedes' postulate
      and relations of betweenness in the process.
\item Draw a line segment. Measure it with your ruler to the nearest 1/16 of an
      inch. Describe your measurement process, using Archimedes' postulate and
      betweenness.
\end{exlist}
\end{multicols}

%========================================================= 5-5
\section*{5--5\quad POINTS ON A LINE}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{5--5\quad Points on a Line}

We have just described the measurement process for getting a number for the
length of a segment. We now turn the question around and ask whether, given a
number, there is a segment with that number for its length. Of course, we would
like this to be true, but our postulates so far do not tell us that it is true.
The process of measurement describes a method for ``sneaking up'' on the point
$B$, but if we start out with a number we are not assured that there is a point
to sneak up on! To have this property, we must postulate it. This postulate
tells us that there are enough points on the line.

\medskip
IV--2. \emph{The completeness postulate.} For every line $l$ and any point $A$
on $l$, and for any positive real number $x$, there is, on a given side of $A$,
a point $B$ such that $\sg{AB} = x$.

\medskip
The name of the last postulate is meant to signify that our lines are complete,
that is, that they have all the points on them we expect them to have.

\exercisegroup{5--8}

\begin{multicols}{2}
\begin{exlist}
\item Draw a segment that is to be the unit segment. Draw another segment that
      is 1.3 units in length.
\item With the unit segment of Exercise 1, draw a segment of length
      $2 + \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{8}$ units.
\end{exlist}
\end{multicols}

%========================================================= 5-6
\section*{5--6\quad LENGTH AND CONGRUENCE}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{5--6\quad Length and Congruence}

When we started talking about congruent segments we had in mind a notion of
size. Now that we have lengths for segments it should turn out that congruent
segments have the same length, and conversely that segments of the same length
are congruent. We now prove these theorems. To do so we need the following
theorem (4--3) that we proved in Chapter 4. \emph{If $AB \cong A'B'$ and $ACB$
and if $C'$ is on the same side of $A'$ as $B'$ and $AC \cong A'C'$, then
$A'C'B'$.}

\medskip\noindent
\textbf{*Theorem 5--1.}\ \emph{If $AB \cong A'B'$, then
$\sg{AB} = \sg{A'B'}$.}
\refstepcounter{theorem}
\par\medskip

\noindent\emph{Proof.} To get the length of segment $AB$, we establish a
sequence of points \emph{between} $A$ and $B$. Let us designate this sequence
by $C_1$, $C_2$, $C_3,\ldots$. Now, consider the corresponding sequence,
$C_1'$, $C_2'$, $C_3',\ldots$, where $AC_1 \cong A'C_1'$,
$AC_2 \cong A'C_2'$, $AC_3 \cong A'C_3',\ldots$, and all the points $C_1'$,
$C_2'$, $C_3',\ldots$ are on the same side of $A'$ as $B'$. Using Theorem
4--3, we see that all the points $C_1'$, $C_2'$, $C_3',\ldots$, are between
$A'$ and $B'$; therefore, this sequence determines the same real number
(decimal) as does the sequence $C_1$, $C_2$, $C_3,\ldots$.

\medskip\noindent
\textbf{*Theorem 5--2.}\ \emph{If $\sg{AB} = \sg{A'B'}$, then
$AB \cong A'B'$.}
\refstepcounter{theorem}
\par\medskip

\noindent\emph{Proof.} This theorem is the converse of Theorem 5--1. We will
prove it by choosing a point $B''$, on the same side of $A$ as $B$, such that
$AB'' \cong A'B'$, and then proving that $B'' = B$ (Fig.~5--8). This will show
that $AB \cong A'B'$. Either $B'' = B$ or $B'' \neq B$. Since
$AB'' \cong A'B'$, then from Theorem 5--1 $\sg{AB''} = \sg{A'B'}$. We are given
that $\sg{AB} = \sg{A'B'}$. Hence $\sg{AB''} = \sg{AB}$. Thus we must show that
if $B'' \neq B$, we cannot have $\sg{AB''} = \sg{A'B'}$. But if $B'' \neq B$,
then, if the unit segment is smaller than $BB''$, the corresponding Archimedes
integers for $AB$ and $AB''$ would be different. This would lead to different
lengths for $AB$ and $AB''$. Hence $B''$ must be the same as $B$ and
$AB \cong A'B'$.

\FIGVEIGHT

These two theorems give us the right to use the words ``the same length'' in
place of ``congruent.'' Therefore we can use everyday language in talking about
congruence of segments.

\exercisegroup{5--9}

\begin{multicols}{2}
\begin{exlist}
\item $AB \cong CD$ and $CD \cong EF$, and $\sg{AB} = 7.26$ inches. What is
      $\sg{EF}$?
\item If $\sg{PQ}$ is 1.23 ft, and $VU \cong RS$, and $\sg{RS} = 1.23$ ft, is
      $QP \cong VU$?
\item If $AB \cong CD$, $CD \cong EF$, $EF \cong GH$, is $\sg{AB} = \sg{GH}$?
\item An isosceles triangle can be defined now in two ways. State the two
      definitions.
\end{exlist}
\end{multicols}

%========================================================= 5-7
\section*{5--7\quad MORE ABOUT INEQUALITIES}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{5--7\quad More about Inequalities}

In Chapter 4 we defined $>$ and $<$ for segments. In this chapter (Section
5--3) we defined $>$ and $<$ for numbers. Since ``same length'' means
``congruent,'' it should also be true that if $AB > CD$, then
$\sg{AB} > \sg{CD}$, and conversely.

\medskip\noindent
\textbf{*Theorem 5--3.}\ \emph{If $AB > CD$ then $\sg{AB} > \sg{CD}$, and
conversely, if $\sg{AB} > \sg{CD}$ then $AB > CD$.}
\refstepcounter{theorem}
\par\medskip

\noindent\emph{Proof.} The theorem could also be stated as ``$AB > CD$ if and
only if $\sg{AB} > \sg{CD}$.'' Or, again, as ``If $AB > CD$ then
$\sg{AB} > \sg{CD}$, and conversely.'' We first prove that $AB > CD$ implies
$\sg{AB} > \sg{CD}$. The hypothesis, $AB > CD$, means that if $E$ is on the
same side of $C$ as $D$, and $AB \cong CE$, then $D$ is between $C$ and $E$.
(See Fig.~5--9.) By Theorem 5--1, $\sg{AB} = \sg{CE}$. In the measurement
process, if the unit is chosen smaller than $DE$, the corresponding Archimedes'
integers for $CD$ and $CE$ will be different, and in fact the integer for $CD$
will be smaller than that for $CE$. Hence $\sg{CD} < \sg{CE}$ and, since
$\sg{CE} = \sg{AB}$, $\sg{CD} < \sg{AB}$.

\FIGVNINE

The converse is proved in a similar manner. We have given that
$\sg{AB} > \sg{CD}$. Choose $E$, on the same side of $C$ as $D$, such that
$AB \cong CE$. By Theorem 5--1, $\sg{AB} = \sg{CE}$. Now either $CDE$,
$D = E$, or $CED$. (Why?) We cannot have $D = E$. (Why?) An argument like the
first part of the proof will show we cannot have $CED$. Hence we must have
$CDE$. It follows from the definition of ``less than'' for segments that
$CD < CE \cong AB$.

\exercisegroup{5--10}

\begin{multicols}{2}
\begin{exlist}
\item If $ABC$ and $\sg{AB} = 5$, what can you say about $\sg{AC}$?
\item If $AB > EF$ and $\sg{EF} = 4$, what can you say about $\sg{AB}$?
\item If $AB > CD > EF$, what can you say about $\sg{AB}$ and $\sg{EF}$?
\item If $ABCD$, what can you say about $\sg{AD}$ and $\sg{BC}$?
\item If $\sg{AB} > \sg{AC}$, and $C$ is a point on the line containing $A$ and
      $B$, and $C$ lies on the same side of $A$ as $B$, where is the point $C$?
\end{exlist}
\end{multicols}

%========================================================= 5-8
\section*{5--8\quad CHANGE OF SCALE}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{5--8\quad Change of Scale}

In measurement we choose a fixed segment for a unit of length. What happens if
a different segment is chosen for the unit? This is a familiar situation
because we are all used to dealing with inches, feet, yards, or miles to
measure length. In Fig.~5--10, if $CD$ is the unit, the length of $AB$ is 3. If
$ED$ is the unit, the length of $AB$ is 6. This illustrates the following
theorem.

\FIGVTEN

\medskip\noindent
\textbf{Theorem 5--4.}\ \emph{If $\sg{AB} = x$ when $CD$ is the unit, and if
$\sg{CD} = y$ when $EF$ is the unit, then $AB = xy$ when $EF$ is the unit.}
\refstepcounter{theorem}
\par\medskip

We will not give the proof of this theorem for arbitrary $x$ and $y$ because it
is long to write out and quite hard if $y$ is an irrational number. But if $y$
is an integer, the proof is very easy and is really clear from Fig.~5--10,
where $y = 2$.

\exercisegroup{5--11}

\begin{multicols}{2}
\begin{exlist}
\item $\sg{AB} = 5$ when $CD$ is the unit, and $\sg{CD} = 2.3$ when $EF$ is the
      unit. What is $\sg{AB}$ when $EF$ is the unit?
\item The width of the room is 14 ft. What is the width in inches? How does
      this follow from Theorem 5--4?
\item One kilometer is 1000 meters. One meter is 100 centimeters. How many
      centimeters in a kilometer? Show how this follows from Theorem 5--4.
\item $\sg{PQ} = 6.5$ when $\sg{RS} = 1$. $\sg{RS} = \frac{1}{2}$ when
      $\sg{UV} = 1$. What is $\sg{PQ}$ when $\sg{UV} = 1$?
\item If $CD < EF$, how does $\sg{AB}$ with unit $CD$ compare with $\sg{AB}$
      with unit $EF$? In other words, if we use two different units and compute
      two lengths for one segment, does the smaller unit give the smaller or
      the larger length?
\end{exlist}
\end{multicols}

%========================================================= Review
\Vhead{Review of Chapter 5}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Review of Chapter 5}
\markboth{REVIEW OF CHAPTER 5}{}

\begin{exlist}
\item In this chapter we have given definitions of the following: real number,
      rational number, irrational number, positive integer, greater than, less
      than, the process of measurement. Be sure you know these definitions.
\item This chapter has two new postulates, Archimedes' postulate and the
      completeness postulate. Go over them again and be sure you see what they
      mean.
\item In this chapter we have proved the following theorems. Study them again
      to be sure you know what they say. You should be able to state clearly
      the facts upon which each proof depends.
\end{exlist}

\begin{align*}
(AB \cong CD) &\iffx \sg{AB} = \sg{CD},\\
(AB > CD) &\iffx \sg{AB} > \sg{CD},\\
(AB < CD) &\iffx \sg{AB} < \sg{CD}.
\end{align*}

\begin{note}
In this chapter we have shown that congruence is equivalent to equality of
length. From this point on in our development of geometry you may use the
ordinary language of length in speaking of congruence.
\end{note}

%========================================================= Algebra review
\Vhead{Algebra Review}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Algebra Review}

\begin{exlist}
\item Segment $XY$ has a length of 28 units. Point $T$ is between $X$ and $Y$
      and $\sg{XT} = \sg{YT} + 9$. Determine the lengths of $XT$ and $YT$.
\item Points $R$, $T$, and $S$ are in this order on a line. Segment $RT$ is
      twice as long as segment $TS$. The difference in their lengths is 11.
      Find the length of $RS$.
\item Points $A$, $B$, and $C$ are on one line. The length of $AC$ is 12 more
      than that of $AB$. The length of $BC$ is four times the length of $AB$.
      Find the lengths of $AB$ and $AC$ if (a) $A$ is between $B$ and $C$, and
      (b) $B$ is between $A$ and $C$.
\item Points $A$, $B$, $C$, and $D$ are in this order on one line.
      $\sg{BC} = \sg{AB} + 4$; $\sg{CD} = \sg{AB} + \sg{BC}$; $\sg{AD} = 32$.
      Find $\sg{AB}$.
\item The length of $XY$ is $\frac{2}{3}$ of the length of $XZ$. The length of
      $XZ$ is $\frac{3}{5}$ of the length of $YZ$. If these three points are
      collinear: (a) What is the order of the points on $l$? (b) Express
      $\sg{XY}$ as a fraction of $\sg{YZ}$. (c) Determine $\sg{XY}$ if
      $\sg{XZ} - \sg{XY} = 6$.
\item The point $M$ is the midpoint of segment $AB$, $N$ is the midpoint of
      $MB$, and $O$ is the midpoint of $NB$. If $\sg{AN} - \sg{NO} = 20$, find
      the length of $AB$.
\item $\sg{AC} = 2\sg{AB}$, $\sg{AB} + \sg{BC} = \sg{AC} + 2$. If
      $\sg{AB} > 1$, prove that the three points $A$, $B$, and $C$ are not on
      one line.
\item A square and equilateral triangle have equal perimeters. The length of a
      side of the triangle exceeds the length of a side of the square by six
      inches. Find the perimeter of each.
\item The sum of the perimeters of a square and a rectangle is 36 ft. The
      rectangle is twice as long as it is wide, and the width of the rectangle
      is 1 ft more than the length of a side of the square. Find the dimensions
      of each.
\item The point $B$ is the midpoint of segment $AC$. Point $X$ is between $B$
      and $C$, and $\sg{BX} = 3$ inches. Show that a square having a side
      congruent to $AB$ has an area of 9 in$^2$ more than a rectangle with
      sides congruent to $AX$ and $XC$.
\end{exlist}
\clearpage

\setcounter{chapter}{6}

\chapter*{\raggedright\Huge CONGRUENCE OF\\ANGLES AND TRIANGLES}
\markboth{CONGRUENCE OF ANGLES AND TRIANGLES}{}
\addcontentsline{toc}{chapter}{6.\ Congruence of Angles and Triangles}
\vspace{-1em}\noindent\rule{\linewidth}{0.6pt}\vspace{1em}
\figurekey

%========================================================= 6-1
\section*{6--1\quad INTRODUCTION}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{6--1\quad Introduction}

In the last two chapters we have been concerned with congruence of segments
only. But we also have a feeling for size of an angle---and, in fact, in
Chapter 1 we used a protractor to measure angles. If our geometry is to be
like the world of our experience, we must include in it postulates that will
enable us to compare the sizes of angles. These postulates form Postulate
Group V. There are four postulates in the group, and we take them up one at a
time. As in Chapter 4, we shall use the word ``congruent'' to give the idea of
\emph{the same size}.

%========================================================= 6-2
\section*{6--2\quad POSTULATE V--1, THE EXISTENCE POSTULATE FOR ANGLES}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{6--2\quad Postulate V--1, the existence postulate for angles}

This first postulate of Group V tells of the existence of angles congruent to
a given angle. Remember to think of the word ``congruent'' as meaning
\emph{the same size}.

\medskip
V--1 If $\ang{A}$ is not a straight angle, and if $r\VIpr$ is a ray from
$A\VIpr$ on a line $l\VIpr$, then on a given side of $l\VIpr$, there is exactly
one ray $s\VIpr$ from $A\VIpr$ such that the angle $A\VIpr$, with sides
$r\VIpr$ and $s\VIpr$, is congruent to angle $A$ (Fig.~6--1). We write this as
$\ang{A\VIpr} \cong \ang{A}$. If $\ang{A}$ is a straight angle, then the
straight angle at $A\VIpr$, with one side $r\VIpr$, is the only angle with one
side $r\VIpr$ congruent to angle $A$.
\medskip

\FIGVIONE

\exercisegroup{6--1}
\begin{multicols}{2}
\begin{exlist}
\item If $\ang{A}$ is not a straight angle, how many angles with side $r\VIpr$
  are congruent to $\ang{A}$? How many if $\ang{A}$ is a straight angle?
\item In a figure like 6--2 draw the possible positions of the side $s\VIpr$
  such that $\ang{A\VIpr} \cong \ang{A}$.
\item In a figure like 6--3, draw all possible positions of $s\VIpr$ such that
  $\ang{A\VIpr} \cong \ang{A}$.
\item If in Fig.~6--4, $A$ is a straight angle and $r\VIpr$ is a ray from
  $A\VIpr$, draw an angle, with one side $r\VIpr$, that is congruent to $A$.
  Is it the only such angle?
\item If $\ang{O}$ is a straight angle and $\ang{O\VIpr} \cong \ang{O}$, is
  $\ang{O\VIpr}$ a straight angle? Why?
\end{exlist}
\end{multicols}

\FIGVITWOTHREEFOUR

%========================================================= 6-3
\section*{6--3\quad POSTULATE V--2, THE THREE-PART ANGLE POSTULATE}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{6--3\quad Postulate V--2, the three-part angle postulate}

The next postulate is for angles what Postulate III--2 is for segments. It may
seem odd to have to state such seemingly obvious things, but remember we are
dealing with those imaginary things called points and lines, and so we must
state \emph{all} the properties we need.

\medskip
\noindent
\begin{tabular}{@{}p{2.2em}@{}p{0.86\linewidth}@{}}
V--2 & (a)\ \ $\ang{A} \cong \ang{A}$.\ \ (Congruence of angles is reflexive.)\\[2pt]
 & (b)\ \ If $\ang{A} \cong \ang{B}$, then $\ang{B} \cong \ang{A}$.
   (Congruence of angles is symmetric.)\\[2pt]
 & (c)\ \ If $\ang{A} \cong \ang{B}$, and $\ang{B} \cong \ang{C}$, then
   $\ang{A} \cong \ang{C}$. (Congruence of angles is transitive.)
\end{tabular}
\medskip

\exercisegroup{6--2}
\begin{multicols}{2}
\begin{exlist}
\item State each part of Postulate V--2 in words.
\item If $\ang{E} \cong \ang{F}$, and $\ang{F} \cong \ang{G}$, and
  $\ang{G} \cong \ang{H}$, show, by using part (c) of Postulate V--2, that
  $\ang{E} \cong \ang{H}$.
\item If $\ang{R} \cong \ang{S}$ and $\ang{T} \cong \ang{S}$, prove that
  $\ang{R} \cong \ang{T}$.
\item[\stex 4.] Use Postulate V--1 and (b) and (c) of Postulate V--2 to prove
  that for every $\ang{A}$, $\ang{A} \cong \ang{A}$.
\end{exlist}
\end{multicols}

%========================================================= 6-4
\section*{6--4\quad POSTULATE V--3, THE ADDITION AND SUBTRACTION OF ANGLES POSTULATE}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{6--4\quad Postulate V--3, the addition and subtraction of angles postulate}

The next postulate does for angles what Postulate III--3 does for segments. It
enables us to ``add'' and ``subtract'' angles. To avoid a complicated statement
in words, we explain the postulate by using Fig.~6--5, where the side common to
$\ang{B}$ and $\ang{C}$, except the vertex, is in the interior of $\ang{A}$,
and the same for $\ang{A\VIpr}$, $\ang{B\VIpr}$, and $\ang{C\VIpr}$.

\FIGVIFIVE

\medskip
\noindent
V--3 If the angles in any two of the pairs $\ang{A}$ and $\ang{A\VIpr}$,
$\ang{B}$ and $\ang{B\VIpr}$, $\ang{C}$ and $\ang{C\VIpr}$ are congruent to
each other, then the angles of the third pair are also congruent to each other.
In other words:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*), leftmargin=2.6em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=3pt]
\item If $\ang{A} \cong \ang{A\VIpr}$ and $\ang{B} \cong \ang{B\VIpr}$, then
  $\ang{C} \cong \ang{C\VIpr}$.
\item If $\ang{B} \cong \ang{B\VIpr}$ and $\ang{C} \cong \ang{C\VIpr}$, then
  $\ang{A} \cong \ang{A\VIpr}$.
\item If $\ang{C} \cong \ang{C\VIpr}$ and $\ang{A} \cong \ang{A\VIpr}$, then
  $\ang{B} \cong \ang{B\VIpr}$.
\end{enumerate}
\noindent The angle $A$ may be a straight angle.
\medskip

\exercisegroup{6--3}
\begin{multicols}{2}
\begin{exlist}
\item We have not yet in our geometry studied the measurement of angles in
  degrees. However, in this exercise, use the fact (which will be proved later)
  that angles congruent to each other have the same measure in degrees, and add
  or subtract degree measures as you are accustomed to do. Refer to Fig.~6--6.
  \begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*), leftmargin=2.2em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=3pt]
  \item If $\ang{A}$ is $130^\circ$ and $\ang{B}$ is $45^\circ$, how many
    degrees in $\ang{C}$?
  \item If $\ang{B\VIpr}$ is $41^\circ$ and $\ang{C\VIpr}$ is $75^\circ$, how
    many degrees in $\ang{A\VIpr}$?
  \item If $\ang{A} \cong \ang{A\VIpr}$ and $\ang{A}$ is $150^\circ$, how many
    degrees in $\ang{A\VIpr}$?
  \item If $\ang{A} \cong \ang{A\VIpr}$ and $\ang{C} \cong \ang{C\VIpr}$, are
    $\ang{B}$ and $\ang{B\VIpr}$ congruent to each other?
  \item If $\ang{A}$ is $87^\circ$ and congruent to $\ang{A\VIpr}$, and if
    $\ang{C} \cong \ang{C\VIpr}$ and $\ang{C\VIpr}$ is $33^\circ$, how many
    degrees in $\ang{B}$?
  \end{enumerate}
\item In Fig.~6--7, if $\ang{POR} \cong \ang{SVU}$, and $\ang{QOR} \cong
  \ang{TVU}$, what can you say about $\ang{POQ}$?
\item In Fig.~6--8, if $\ang{BAC} \cong \ang{DAE}$, what can you say about
  $\ang{BAD}$?
\item In Fig.~6--9, if $\ang{SPU} \cong \ang{RPT}$, what can you say about
  $\ang{RPS}$?
\item Is Exercise 2 an example of ``adding'' or ``subtracting'' angles? What
  about Exercises 3 and 4?
\end{exlist}
\end{multicols}

\FIGVISIXSEVEN

\FIGVIEIGHTNINE

Supplementary and adjacent angles were defined in Definition 3--9. The
statement that $\ang{A}$ is \emph{supplementary} to $\ang{B}$ shall mean that
$\ang{A}$ is congruent to an angle that is \emph{supplementary and adjacent} to
$\ang{B}$.

\begin{theorem}
If two angles are congruent to each other, then their supplements are also
congruent to each other.
\end{theorem}

\emph{Proof.} Let the given angles be $A$ and $A\VIpr$, and let their
supplements be $B$ and $B\VIpr$, respectively, as in Fig.~6--10. We are given
that $\ang{A} \cong \ang{A\VIpr}$. Since any two straight angles are congruent
to each other, it follows at once from Postulate V--3 that $\ang{B} \cong
\ang{B\VIpr}$. (Why?)

\FIGVITENELEVENTWELVE

\begin{theorem}
Angles that are vertical to each other are also congruent to each other.
\end{theorem}

\emph{Proof.} Let the angles $A$ and $A\VIpr$ be vertical to each other, as in
Fig.~6--11, and consider $\ang{B}$, one of the other angles formed by the
lines. Then $\ang{B}$ is the supplement of $\ang{A}$ and also the supplement of
$\ang{A\VIpr}$. Since $\ang{B} \cong \ang{B}$, it follows from Theorem 6--1
that $\ang{A} \cong \ang{A\VIpr}$.

\begin{definition}
An angle (Fig.~6--12) that is congruent to its supplement is called a
\emph{right angle}.
\end{definition}

\begin{remark}
Note that the words \emph{congruent}, \emph{vertical}, \emph{equal}, and
\emph{supplementary} refer to relations between two objects, not to their
properties. That is, it makes no sense to say that $\ang{A}$ is a vertical
angle, or a congruent angle, or a supplementary angle. At times, we refer to
two angles $A$ and $B$ as equal angles, or vertical angles, or congruent
angles, etc. What we really mean is that $\ang{A}$ is equal to $\ang{B}$,
$\ang{A}$ is vertical to $\ang{B}$, $\ang{A}$ is congruent to $\ang{B}$, etc.
It is important to distinguish between properties and relations.
\end{remark}

\item[\stex 4.] An angle is congruent to a right angle. Show that it, too, is a
  right angle.
\item[5.] In Fig.~6--15, the line $CD$ bisects $\ang{AOB}$. Show that it also
  bisects $\ang{EOF}$. (By ``bisect'' we mean that $\ang{AOC} \cong \ang{COB}$.)
\item[6.] Decide whether the following words refer to properties or relations:
  perpendicular, parallel, vertex, altitude, greater than, angle, segment,
  median, right (angle), straight (angle), bisector.
\end{exlist}
\end{multicols}

%========================================================= 6-5
\section*{6--5\quad POSTULATE V--4, THE SIDE-ANGLE-SIDE POSTULATE}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{6--5\quad Postulate V--4, the side-angle-side postulate}

This postulate (abbreviated S.A.S.) is one that combines congruence of segments
with congruence of angles. Up to this point, we have the two kinds of
congruence but no relationship between them. This is the connecting link that
will enable us to prove many theorems.

\medskip
\noindent
V--4 If two triangles, $\tri{ABC}$ and $\tri{A\VIpr B\VIpr C\VIpr}$, are such
that $AB \cong A\VIpr B\VIpr$, $AC \cong A\VIpr C\VIpr$, and $\ang{A} \cong
\ang{A\VIpr}$, then $\ang{B} \cong \ang{B\VIpr}$ and $\ang{C} \cong
\ang{C\VIpr}$ (Fig.~6--16).
\medskip

\FIGVISIXTEEN

This postulate tells us that if two triangles have two sides of one congruent
to two sides of the other, and if the angles formed by these two sides (called
the \emph{included} angles) are congruent to each other, then the other pairs
of corresponding angles are congruent.

%========================================================= 6-6
\section*{6--6\quad ISOSCELES TRIANGLES}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{6--6\quad Isosceles triangles}

We can now prove a theorem about isosceles triangles, for which we need a
definition. The definition of isosceles triangle is the same as that given in
Chapter 1, Exercise Group 1--4:

\begin{definition}
A triangle is called \emph{isosceles} if two of its sides are congruent (of
equal length). The \emph{base angles} of the triangle are those opposite the
congruent sides.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}
In every isosceles triangle, the base angles are congruent to each other.
\end{theorem}

\emph{Proof.} Consider any isosceles triangle, and label the vertices in two
different ways, as shown in Fig.~6--32. Let $AB \cong AC$. Let us look at
the triangle both as $\tri{ABC}$ and as $\tri{A\VIpr B\VIpr C\VIpr}$. We have
$AB \cong AC \cong A\VIpr B\VIpr$, and $AC \cong AB = A\VIpr C\VIpr$, and
$\ang{A} \cong \ang{A\VIpr}$. Therefore, by the S.A.S. postulate, $\ang{B}
\cong \ang{B\VIpr}$, that is, $\ang{B} \cong \ang{C}$.

This proof is quite interesting because it illustrates very well how good
notation can help. In the proof we look at the same triangle in two different
ways, and once we have done this, the proof is very short.

\FIGVITHIRTYTWO

\begin{definition}
A \emph{midpoint} of a segment $AB$ is a point $M$ of the segment, such that
$AM \cong MB$.
\end{definition}

%========================================================= 6-7
\section*{6--7\quad CONGRUENCE OF TRIANGLES}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{6--7\quad Congruence of triangles}

We now define congruence for triangles and prove some theorems.

\begin{definition}
Two triangles are said to be \emph{congruent} to each other if they can be
labeled $\tri{ABC}$ and $\tri{A\VIpr B\VIpr C\VIpr}$, such that
$AB \cong A\VIpr B\VIpr$, $AC \cong A\VIpr C\VIpr$, $BC \cong B\VIpr C\VIpr$,
$\ang{A} \cong \ang{A\VIpr}$, $\ang{B} \cong \ang{B\VIpr}$, and $\ang{C} \cong
\ang{C\VIpr}$. We then write $\tri{ABC} \cong \tri{A\VIpr B\VIpr C\VIpr}$ and
read this as ``triangle $ABC$ is congruent to triangle $A\VIpr B\VIpr
C\VIpr$.'' $\ang{A}$ corresponds to $\ang{A\VIpr}$, $\ang{B}$ to
$\ang{B\VIpr}$, side $AC$ to side $A\VIpr C\VIpr$, etc.
\end{definition}

\exercise{6--7}
Prove that congruence of triangles is transitive.

\begin{theorem}
If the vertices of two triangles may be labeled $A$, $B$, $C$ and $A\VIpr$,
$B\VIpr$, $C\VIpr$, such that $AB \cong A\VIpr B\VIpr$, $AC \cong A\VIpr
C\VIpr$, $\ang{A} \cong \ang{A\VIpr}$, then $\tri{ABC} \cong \tri{A\VIpr
B\VIpr C\VIpr}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{remark}
This is the first of the three congruence theorems for triangles. It may also
be stated as follows: \emph{if two triangles are such that two sides and the
included angle of one are congruent, respectively, to two sides and the
included angle of the other, then the triangles are congruent.} This theorem
is often called the ``side-angle-side theorem'' and is abbreviated S.A.S.
\end{remark}

\emph{Proof.} From the S.A.S. postulate, we know that $\ang{B} \cong
\ang{B\VIpr}$ and $\ang{C} \cong \ang{C\VIpr}$. It only remains to be shown
that the third sides are congruent, that is, that $BC \cong B\VIpr C\VIpr$. We
prove this by considering the point $D\VIpr$ on ray $C\VIpr B\VIpr$, such that
$CB \cong C\VIpr D\VIpr$, as in Fig.~6--43, and then showing that $D\VIpr =
B\VIpr$.

\FIGVIFORTYTHREE

\begin{steps}
\step{There is a point $D\VIpr$ on the ray $C\VIpr B\VIpr$ such that $CB \cong
      C\VIpr D\VIpr$.}{Existence postulate for segments.}
\step{$AC \cong A\VIpr C\VIpr$, and $AB \cong A\VIpr B\VIpr$.}{Given.}
\step{$\ang{B\VIpr A\VIpr C\VIpr} \cong \ang{BAC}$.}{Given.}
\step{$\ang{C} \cong \ang{C\VIpr}$, and $\ang{B} \cong \ang{B\VIpr}$.}{S.A.S. postulate.}
\step{$\ang{BAC} \cong \ang{D\VIpr A\VIpr C\VIpr}$.}{By S.A.S. postulate, considering
      $\tri{ACB}$ and $\tri{A\VIpr C\VIpr D\VIpr}$.}
\step{Ray $A\VIpr B\VIpr$ is the same as the ray $A\VIpr D\VIpr$.}{Existence postulate for angles.}
\step{$B\VIpr = D\VIpr$.}{The lines $A\VIpr B\VIpr$ and
      $B\VIpr C\VIpr$ intersect in exactly one point by Theorem 3--1. This
      point is $B\VIpr$ and is also $D\VIpr$.}
\step{$BC \cong B\VIpr C\VIpr$.}{Statements 1 and 7.}
\step{$\tri{ABC} \cong \tri{A\VIpr B\VIpr C\VIpr}$.}{Definition 6--4.}
\end{steps}

In the exercises that follow we will make use of the congruence theorems. In
some exercises it will be convenient to know that \emph{``halves'' of congruent
segments are congruent to each other}. That is, if $AB \cong CD$ and $M$ and $N$
are midpoints of $AB$ and $CD$ respectively, then $AM \cong CN$. To see this we
note that $\sg{AB} = \sg{CD}$ and by the properties of numbers $\sg{AM} =
\sg{CN}$ so that $AM \cong CN$.

%========================================================= 6-8
\section*{6--8\quad THE SECOND CONGRUENCE THEOREM}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{6--8\quad The second congruence theorem}

The first congruence theorem was the side-angle-side theorem (S.A.S.). The
second one says that two triangles are congruent if two angles and the included
side of one are, respectively, congruent to two angles and the included side of
the other. This theorem is called the ``angle-side-angle theorem'' and is
abbreviated A.S.A.

\begin{theorem}
If two triangles $\tri{ABC}$ and $\tri{A\VIpr B\VIpr C\VIpr}$ are such that
$\ang{A} \cong \ang{A\VIpr}$, $\ang{C} \cong \ang{C\VIpr}$, and $AC \cong
A\VIpr C\VIpr$, then $\tri{ABC} \cong \tri{A\VIpr B\VIpr C\VIpr}$.
\end{theorem}

\FIGVIFIFTYFIVE

\emph{Proof.} We consider the point $D\VIpr$ on the ray $A\VIpr B\VIpr$
(Fig.~6--55), such that $AB \cong A\VIpr D\VIpr$. Then it is true that
$\tri{ABC} \cong \tri{A\VIpr D\VIpr C\VIpr}$. (Why?) Then, if $D\VIpr \neq
B\VIpr$, we have both $\ang{D\VIpr C\VIpr A\VIpr}$ and $\ang{B\VIpr C\VIpr
A\VIpr}$ congruent to $\ang{C}$. This is impossible, so $B\VIpr = D\VIpr$.

\begin{steps}
\step{There is a point $D\VIpr$ on the ray $A\VIpr B\VIpr$, such that $AB \cong
      A\VIpr D\VIpr$.}{Existence postulate for segments.}
\step{$\ang{A} \cong \ang{A\VIpr}$, $AC \cong A\VIpr C\VIpr$.}{Given.}
\step{$\ang{C} \cong \ang{D\VIpr C\VIpr A\VIpr}$.}{S.A.S. postulate, applied to
      $\tri{ABC}$ and $\tri{A\VIpr D\VIpr C\VIpr}$.}
\step{$\ang{C} \cong \ang{B\VIpr C\VIpr A\VIpr}$.}{Given.}
\step{Ray $C\VIpr D\VIpr$ $=$ ray $C\VIpr B\VIpr$.}{Existence postulate for angles.}
\step{$D\VIpr = B\VIpr$.}{Two lines intersect in at most
      one point.}
\step{$\tri{ABC} \cong \tri{A\VIpr B\VIpr C\VIpr}$.}{S.A.S. theorem.}
\end{steps}

In Section 6--6 we proved that the base angles of an isosceles triangle are
congruent. We can now easily prove the converse.

\begin{theorem}
If a triangle has two angles congruent to each other, then the sides opposite
these angles are congruent.
\end{theorem}

\emph{Proof.} Suppose that the triangle is $\tri{ABC}$, and that $\ang{A} \cong
\ang{C}$. Let the vertices be labeled $A\VIpr$, $B\VIpr$, $C\VIpr$, as in
Fig.~6--68. Then we have $\ang{A} \cong \ang{C} \cong \ang{A\VIpr}$, and
$\ang{C} \cong \ang{A} \cong \ang{C\VIpr}$, and $AC \cong CA \cong A\VIpr
C\VIpr$. Hence by the A.S.A. congruence theorem, $\tri{ABC} \cong \tri{A\VIpr
B\VIpr C\VIpr}$. Therefore $AB \cong A\VIpr B\VIpr \cong CB$.

\FIGVISIXTYEIGHT

Prove that an equiangular triangle is equilateral.

%========================================================= 6-9
\section*{6--9\quad THE THIRD CONGRUENCE THEOREM}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{6--9\quad The third congruence theorem}

The two previous congruence theorems were the S.A.S. and A.S.A. theorems. The
third of the three fundamental congruence theorems states that two triangles
are congruent if the sides of one are congruent to the sides of the other. It
is called the ``side-side-side theorem'' and is abbreviated S.S.S.

\begin{theorem}
If the sides of one triangle are congruent, respectively, to the sides of
another triangle, then the triangles are congruent.
\end{theorem}

\FIGVISIXTYNINE

\emph{Proof.} Suppose that the triangles are labeled $\tri{ABC}$ and
$\tri{A\VIpr B\VIpr C\VIpr}$, as in Fig.~6--69(a) and 6--69(b), and that $AB
\cong A\VIpr B\VIpr$, $AC \cong A\VIpr C\VIpr$, and $BC \cong B\VIpr C\VIpr$.
We have only to prove that the angles are congruent. There is a ray $AD$, as in
Fig.~6--69(c), from $A$ on the opposite side of $AC$ from $B$, such that
$\ang{DAC} \cong \ang{A\VIpr}$. On $AD$, there is a point $E$, such that $AE
\cong A\VIpr B\VIpr$.

\begin{steps}
\step{$\ang{EAC} \cong \ang{A\VIpr}$.}{The ray $AE$ was chosen this way.}
\step{$AE \cong A\VIpr B\VIpr$.}{$E$ was so chosen.}
\step{$AC \cong A\VIpr C\VIpr$.}{Given.}
\step{$\tri{AEC} \cong \tri{A\VIpr B\VIpr C\VIpr}$.}{S.A.S. theorem.}
\end{steps}

Now consider the segment $BE$ and the triangles $ABE$ and $BEC$, as in
Fig.~6--70.

\FIGVISEVENTY

\begin{steps}
\stepx{5}{$\tri{ABE}$ is isosceles.}{$AB \cong A\VIpr B\VIpr
      \cong AE$.}
\stepx{6}{$\ang{1} \cong \ang{3}$.}{Statement 5 and Theorem 6--3.}
\stepx{7}{$\ang{2} \cong \ang{4}$.}{Same argument as used for
      $\ang{1}$ and $\ang{3}$.}
\stepx{8}{$\ang{B} \cong \ang{E}$.}{Addition of angles postulate.}
\stepx{9}{$\tri{ABC} \cong \tri{AEC}$.}{S.A.S. theorem.}
\stepx{10}{$\tri{ABC} \cong \tri{A\VIpr B\VIpr C\VIpr}$.}{Statements 4 and 9.}
\end{steps}

\begin{remark}
In our proof, we have tacitly assumed that $BE$ intersects the segment $AC$ at
a point between $A$ and $C$. This need not be the case. We could have either
Fig.~6--71(a) or 6--71(b).

\par\medskip\noindent\emph{Problem.} Prove both cases.
\end{remark}

\FIGVISEVENTYONE

%========================================================= 6-10
\section*{6--10\quad RIGHT ANGLES}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{6--10\quad Right angles}

In Definition 6--1 we defined right angles, but so far \emph{we do not know
that there are such angles}. We now show how to use our congruence theorem
(S.A.S.) to show that there is a right angle in our geometry.

\FIGVININETYTHREE

\emph{Proof.} On a line $l$, choose a point $O$ and let $\ang{AOB}$ be an angle
(not straight) with one side on $l$ (Fig.~6--93). Now consider the angle
congruent to $\ang{AOB}$, with vertex $O$, one side $OB$ on the line $l$ and
the other on the opposite side of $l$ from $A$. Choose the point $A\VIpr$ on
this last side, such that $OA \cong OA\VIpr$. Because $A$ and $A\VIpr$ are on
opposite sides of $l$, the segment $AA\VIpr$ intersects the line in some point
$C$. There are three cases to consider, as shown in Fig.~6--94.

\FIGVININETYFOUR

If $C$ is on the same side of $O$ as $B$, then by the S.A.S. theorem,
$\tri{AOC} \cong \tri{A\VIpr OC}$. Hence $\ang{OCA} \cong \ang{OCA\VIpr}$.
Since these angles are congruent and supplementary to each other, they are
right angles. In case $C = O$, we have $\ang{AOB} \cong \ang{A\VIpr OB}$, and
hence they are right angles. If $C$ is on the opposite side of $O$ from $B$,
then the angles $AOC$ and $A\VIpr OC$ are congruent. (Why?) We may apply the
S.A.S. congruence theorem. $\ang{ACO} \cong \ang{A\VIpr CO}$, and these are
right angles.

\item If, in the figure, $AB \cong AD$, and $BC \cong CD$, prove that

\end{exlist}
\end{multicols}

%========================================================= 6-11
\section*{6--11\quad INEQUALITIES FOR ANGLES}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{6--11\quad Inequalities for angles}

Even before studying geometry you used angles of the same size and compared
angles of different sizes (by saying, for example, that one angle is larger
than another). In this section, we see how to compare the sizes of angles. To
do this, we have to define $>$ (is greater than) and $<$ (is less than) for
angles. The idea we use in forming this definition is illustrated in
Fig.~6--97. If $\ang{B\VIpr}$ is congruent to $\ang{B}$, and $\ang{B\VIpr}$ and
$\ang{A}$ are as drawn (that is, the other side of $\ang{B\VIpr}$ is \emph{in
the interior} of $\ang{A}$), then we would say that $\ang{B} < \ang{A}$. In
Fig.~6--97, we have, so to speak, ``moved'' $\ang{B}$ to the position of
$\ang{B\VIpr}$ for comparison. Notice how the definition below parallels the
definition of ``greater than'' and ``less than'' for segments.

\FIGVININETYSEVEN

\begin{definition}
Let $A$ and $B$ be any angles not straight angles. Let $\ang{B\VIpr}$ be an
angle congruent to $\ang{B}$, such that one side of $\ang{B\VIpr}$ is the same
as the first side of $\ang{A}$, and the other side of $\ang{B\VIpr}$ and the
second side of $\ang{A}$ both lie on the same side of the first side of
$\ang{A}$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*), leftmargin=2.2em, itemsep=2pt, topsep=3pt]
\item If the second side of $\ang{B\VIpr}$ is interior to $\ang{A}$, we say
  that $\ang{B} < \ang{A}$. (See Fig.~6--98.)
\item If the second side of $\ang{B\VIpr}$ is exterior to $\ang{A}$, we say
  that $\ang{B} > \ang{A}$. (See Fig.~6--99.)
\item If $\ang{A}$ is a straight angle, and $\ang{B}$ is not, we say that
  $\ang{A} > \ang{B}$ and that $\ang{B} < \ang{A}$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition}

\FIGVININETYEIGHTNINETYNINE

Our intuition tells us that if $\ang{B} < \ang{A}$, then $\ang{A} > \ang{B}$,
and if $\ang{B} > \ang{A}$, then $\ang{A} < \ang{B}$. These statements require
proof. Since the proofs of these statements are essentially the same, we prove
only the first.

\begin{theorem}
If $\ang{B}$ and $\ang{A}$ are two angles, such that $\ang{B} < \ang{A}$, then
$\ang{A} > \ang{B}$.
\end{theorem}

\VIstarnote{*This proof is difficult. If the teacher wishes, Theorem 6--8 may
be treated as a postulate.}

\stex\emph{Proof.} Figure 6--100 shows that $\ang{B} < \ang{A}$. To show that
$\ang{A} > \ang{B}$, we must show that the second side of $\ang{A\VIpr}$ is in
the exterior of $\ang{B}$, as in Fig.~6--101.

\FIGVIONEHUNDREDONEHUNDREDONE

\FIGVIONEHUNDREDTWO

Choose points $D$ and $E$ on the sides of $\ang{A}$ and points $D\VIpr$ and
$E\VIpr$ on the sides of $\ang{A\VIpr}$ such that $AD \cong BD\VIpr$ and $AE
\cong BE\VIpr$. (See Fig.~6--102.) $DE$ intersects the second side of
$\ang{B\VIpr}$ in some point $F$ between $D$ and $E$ because the second side of
$\ang{B\VIpr}$ is in the interior of $\ang{A}$. $\tri{ADE} \cong \tri{BD\VIpr
E\VIpr}$ by the S.A.S. theorem, and hence $DE \cong D\VIpr E\VIpr$. Choose
$F\VIpr$ between $D\VIpr$ and $E\VIpr$, such that $DF \cong D\VIpr F\VIpr$.
This is possible because $D\VIpr E\VIpr \cong DE > DF$. The ray $BF\VIpr$ is in
the interior of $\ang{A\VIpr}$. (Why?) $\ang{D} \cong \ang{D\VIpr}$, and hence
$\tri{FDA} \cong \tri{F\VIpr D\VIpr B}$. $\ang{DAF} \cong \ang{D\VIpr
BF\VIpr}$, and $\ang{DAF}$ was given congruent to $\ang{B}$. By the three-part
angle postulate, $\ang{B} \cong \ang{D\VIpr BF\VIpr}$; it follows that the ray
$BF\VIpr$ is the same as the second side of $\ang{B}$. Therefore, the second
side of $\ang{B}$ is interior to $\ang{A\VIpr}$ or, what is the same, the
second side of $\ang{A\VIpr}$ is in the exterior of $\ang{B}$. This completes
the proof that $\ang{A} > \ang{B}$.

\begin{remark}
Theorem 6--8 tells us that we get the same result regardless of whether we
``move'' $B$ to compare with $A$, or ``move'' $A$ to compare with $B$.
\end{remark}

\begin{theorem}
For any two angles $\ang{A}$ and $\ang{B}$, either $\ang{A} < \ang{B}$, or
$\ang{A} \cong \ang{B}$, or $\ang{A} > \ang{B}$; and exactly one of these is
true.
\end{theorem}

\emph{Proof.} If $\ang{A}$ is a straight angle, either $\ang{A} \cong \ang{B}$
and $\ang{B}$ is also a straight angle or, by Definition 6--5, $\ang{A} >
\ang{B}$. Similarly, if $\ang{B}$ is a straight angle, either $\ang{B} \cong
\ang{A}$ or $\ang{B} > \ang{A}$. If neither $\ang{A}$ nor $\ang{B}$ is
straight, then the second side of $\ang{B\VIpr}$ coincides with the second side
of $\ang{A}$, and $\ang{B} \cong \ang{A}$; or the second side of $\ang{B\VIpr}$
is interior to $\ang{A}$, and $\ang{A} > \ang{B}$; or the second side of
$\ang{B\VIpr}$ is exterior to $\ang{A}$, and $\ang{A} < \ang{B}$. Since only
one of these possibilities can hold, the proof is complete.

Some simple properties of inequalities are collected in the following theorem.

\begin{theorem}
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*), leftmargin=2.2em, itemsep=1pt, topsep=3pt]
\item If $\ang{A} \cong \ang{B}$, and $\ang{B} < \ang{C}$, then $\ang{A} < \ang{C}$.
\item If $\ang{A} < \ang{B}$, and $\ang{B} \cong \ang{C}$, then $\ang{A} < \ang{C}$.
\item If $\ang{A} \cong \ang{B}$, and $\ang{B} > \ang{C}$, then $\ang{A} > \ang{C}$.
\item If $\ang{A} < \ang{B}$, and $\ang{B} < \ang{C}$, then $\ang{A} < \ang{C}$.
\item If $\ang{A} \geqq \ang{B}$, and $\ang{B} \geqq \ang{C}$, then
  $\ang{A} \geqq \ang{C}$.*
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

\VIstarnote{*The symbol $\geqq$ means ``greater than or congruent to,'' as in
Chapter 4.}

\emph{Proof of} (a). Since $\ang{B} < \ang{C}$, on ``moving'' $\ang{B}$ to
compare with $\ang{C}$, the second side of $\ang{B\VIpr}$ is interior to
$\ang{C}$. Since $\ang{A} \cong \ang{B}$, the second sides of $\ang{A\VIpr}$
and $\ang{B\VIpr}$ would be the same. Hence $\ang{A} < \ang{C}$. The proofs in
all the other cases are essentially the same.

\exercisegroup{6--13}
\begin{multicols}{2}
\begin{exlist}
\item Can you think of any other properties not included in Theorem 6--10?
  There are several. Write them down. Draw figures to illustrate them.
\item Draw figures to indicate that parts (b) through (e) of Theorem 6--10 are
  true. Be sure you understand how to use Definition 6--5.
\end{exlist}
\end{multicols}

\begin{definition}
An angle less than a right angle is called an \emph{acute} angle. An angle
greater than a right angle is called an \emph{obtuse} angle.
\end{definition}

%========================================================= 6-12
\section*{6--12\quad RIGHT ANGLES AGAIN}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{6--12\quad Right angles again}

We can now use Theorem 6--9 to prove that all right angles are congruent to
each other. It is interesting, from a historical point of view, to know that
Euclid \emph{postulated} this fact. The proof we give below could have been
formulated by Euclid just as well as he formulated other proofs. Not only did
Euclid ignore postulates that were needed (like the betweenness postulates),
but he also introduced postulates that were not needed.

\begin{theorem}
All right angles are congruent to each other.
\end{theorem}

\emph{Proof.} Suppose that two right angles are $\ang{A}$ and $\ang{B}$, and
that their supplements are $\ang{A\VIpr}$ and $\ang{B\VIpr}$, as in
Fig.~6--103(a) and 6--103(b). There are only three possibilities, according to
Theorem 6--9. Either $\ang{A} < \ang{B}$, or $\ang{A} \cong \ang{B}$, or
$\ang{A} > \ang{B}$, and one of these must be true. We will show that $\ang{A}
< \ang{B}$ and $\ang{A} > \ang{B}$ are false. Suppose that $\ang{A} < \ang{B}$,
and that $\ang{B\VIppr}$ is congruent to $\ang{B}$ and located as in
Fig.~6--103(c). Let $B\VIpppr$ be the supplement of $\ang{B\VIppr}$.

\FIGVIONEHUNDREDTHREE

\begin{steps}
\step{$\ang{B\VIppr} \cong \ang{B}$.}{By definition of $\ang{B\VIppr}$.}
\step{$\ang{B\VIpppr}$ is the supplement of $\ang{B\VIppr}$, and
      $\ang{B\VIpr}$ is the supplement of $\ang{B}$.}{By definition of supplement.}
\step{$\ang{B\VIpr} \cong \ang{B\VIpppr}$.}{If angles are congruent, their
      supplements are congruent.}
\step{$\ang{B} \cong \ang{B\VIpr}$.}{$\ang{B}$ is a right angle.}
\step{$\ang{B} \cong \ang{B\VIpppr}$.}{Angle congruence is transitive.}
\step{$\ang{A} < \ang{B}$.}{Hypothesis.}
\step{$\ang{A} < \ang{B\VIpppr}$.}{$\ang{A} < \ang{B} \cong
      \ang{B\VIpppr}$.}
\step{$\ang{B\VIpppr} < \ang{A\VIpr}$.}{The ``second'' side of
      $\ang{B\VIpppr}$ is in the interior of $\ang{A\VIpr}$.}
\step{$\ang{B\VIpppr} < \ang{A}$.}{$\ang{B\VIpppr} < \ang{A\VIpr}
      \cong \ang{A}$.}
\step{$\ang{A} < \ang{A}$.}{Statements 7 and 9.}
\end{steps}

Since $\ang{A} \cong \ang{A}$, we know by Theorem 6--9 that it is impossible
for $\ang{A}$ to be less than itself. Therefore, it is impossible that $\ang{A}
< \ang{B}$. In the same way, it can be shown that it is impossible that
$\ang{B} < \ang{A}$. Therefore, we must have $\ang{A} \cong \ang{B}$. This
completes the proof.

\begin{definition}
Two lines, $l$ and $m$, are said to be \emph{perpendicular} to each other if
they intersect and the angles formed are right angles, as in Fig.~6--104(a).
To indicate that lines are perpendicular we write ``$l \perp m$.''
\end{definition}

\FIGVIONEHUNDREDFOUR

The line $l$ is called the \emph{perpendicular bisector} of the segment $AB$ if
$l \perp AB$ and $l$ passes through the midpoint of $AB$, as in
Fig.~6--104(b). This is written ``$l \perp$ bis $AB$,'' and read ``$l$ is the
perpendicular bisector of $AB$.''

%========================================================= Review
\section*{REVIEW OF CHAPTER 6}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Review of Chapter 6}

In this chapter there are many important ideas and geometric facts. It is most
important that you review the topics listed below. Each topic contains many
ideas, so study each one separately. Then study the whole list to be sure that
you understand how the topics are related.

1. First in importance are the four postulates of Group V. It is not necessary
to memorize the postulates word for word, but you must understand the meaning
of each one so that you will know when you can use it.

2. We also gave several important definitions. Be sure that you know
definitions for the following: right angle, congruent triangles, $>$ and $<$
for angles, acute angle, obtuse angle.

3. Below we list the most important theorems proved in this chapter. You should
be able to prove many of them. In reviewing the proofs of these theorems, first
see whether you can formulate a proof without looking at the text.

\begin{quote}
If two angles are congruent, their supplements are congruent.\\
Vertical angles are congruent.\\
In an isosceles triangle, the base angles are congruent.\\
The first congruence theorem (S.A.S.).\\
For any two angles $\ang{A}$ and $\ang{B}$, exactly one of the following is
true: $\ang{A} > \ang{B}$, $\ang{A} \cong \ang{B}$, $\ang{A} < \ang{B}$.\\
If $\ang{A} \cong \ang{B}$, and $\ang{B} < \ang{C}$, then $\ang{A} < \ang{C}$,
etc.\\
All right angles are congruent.\\
The second congruence theorem (A.S.A.).\\
The third congruence theorem (S.S.S.).
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Review Exercises}
\begin{multicols}{2}
\begin{exlist}
\item Draw an $\ang{A}$. Draw a ray $r$ from a point $O$. Draw the two angles
  congruent to $A$ that have the ray $r$ as one side. See Postulate V--1.
\item If $\ang{A} \cong \ang{D}$, and $\ang{D} \cong \ang{E}$, and $\ang{E}
  \cong \ang{F}$, prove that $\ang{A} \cong \ang{F}$. See Postulate V--2.
\item If in Fig.~6--112, $\ang{A_1} \cong \ang{R}$, and $\ang{A_2} \cong
  \ang{S}$, prove that $\ang{B} \cong \ang{T}$. See Postulate V--3.
\item If in Fig.~6--113, $\ang{A} \cong \ang{B}$, prove that $\ang{C} \cong
  \ang{D}$. What is the converse of this? Is the converse true? What is the
  contrapositive of this? Is it true?

\chapter*{\raggedright\Huge USE OF THE\\CONGRUENCE THEOREMS}
